title: [Chapitre] III. Réseaux via découpages : notes manuscrites (08/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: notes 156-3, 'Réseaux via découpages' (1986). On the previous page Grothendieck begins an axiomatic theory of 'découpages'. This is a combinatorial notion of tame ('modéré') space. There is an ambient set together with a class of tame closed subsets S ('parties modérées fermées', abbreviated Modf). Each such S has a complement C(S) with connected components, and each component A has a boundary Ȧ contained in S. He states two axioms. Dec1 (finiteness): the set of connected components of any U = C(S) is finite. Dec2 (monotonicity): if U = C(S) ⊂ V = C(T), i.e. T ⊂ S, then each component A of U lies in a unique component B of V, and Ȧ ∩ T ⊂ Ḃ.

This page gives Example 1, the 'ordered line'. Let L be an ordered set with the following properties: filtered upward and downward, no greatest or least element, locally filtered both ways, and 'divisible' (read: dense). The insertion 'pour les tot. ordonnés' shows that the working case is a totally ordered set. Such an L is called a 'ligne ordonnée'.

The data are as follows.
- S_0 = P_2(L), the 2-element subsets. These appear to be the elementary boundary configurations, the boundaries of segments, as the next page makes explicit with 'tronçons'.
- Modf(L) = the finite subsets of L.

For T = {t_1 < ... < t_n} in Modf(L), the connected components of L \ T are the n+1 open intervals ]-∞,t_1[, ]t_1,t_2[, ..., ]t_{n-1},t_n[, ]t_n,+∞[. Their boundaries are {t_1}, {t_1,t_2}, ..., {t_{n-1},t_n}, {t_n}.

This verifies Dec1, since there are n+1 components. It also verifies Dec2 implicitly: refining T to S ⊃ T subdivides each interval, and any endpoint of a small interval that lies in T is an endpoint of the big interval containing it.

The page closes with a marginal 'Pb fonctions[?]', apparently a problem to address, perhaps functions or functoriality on such lines. The next page goes on to define tronçons [s,t], ]-∞,s], [s,+∞[ and their boundaries, and 'positions modérées' as finite disjoint unions of mutually tame tronçons. The purpose is to test the découpage axioms on the simplest one-dimensional model, the analogue of the o-minimal line, before building 'réseaux'.
errors: The component computation tacitly requires L to be totally ordered. For a genuinely partial order the complement of a finite set is not a union of intervals. The list of hypotheses (filtered up/down, locally filtered) is redundant for a total order; it suggests Grothendieck had partial orders in mind before restricting with 'pour les tot. ordonnés'.

Density ('divisible') and the absence of extremal elements are needed so that all n+1 components are nonempty, e.g. ]t,t+1[ is empty in Z. This is used but not stated as the reason for the hypotheses.
Dec2 is not explicitly checked on the page, but it does hold for this example.

ideas.what: Axiomatic notion of a 'découpage': tame closed subsets, connected components of their complements with boundaries, a finiteness axiom and a refinement/boundary-compatibility axiom
ideas.modern_name: Combinatorial tame topology; analogous to o-minimal structures / stratified spaces
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck's programme of 'topologie modérée' (Esquisse 1984); o-minimality: van den Dries, Pillay–Steinhorn, Knight (1980s)
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme §5 announces tame topology in general terms; the specific découpage axioms are, as far as I know, only in these unpublished notes

ideas.what: The ordered line as the basic example: finite subsets as tame closed sets, complements decomposed into n+1 open intervals with 1- or 2-point boundaries
ideas.modern_name: Dense linear order without endpoints / o-minimal line (definable subsets of the line are finite unions of points and intervals)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard (o-minimality literature, van den Dries 'Tame topology and o-minimal structures' 1998)

missed.claim: This page is one of the first worked examples of Grothendieck's unpublished axiomatic 'découpage' framework (1986), an alternative, purely combinatorial axiomatization of tame topology. The framework is based on components of complements and boundary-compatibility under refinement rather than on definable sets. The framework as a whole seems undocumented in the literature, though this particular page is routine.
missed.quote: On appelle[?] un tel ensemble une ligne ordonnée ... Modf(L) = parties finies
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historians and model theorists comparing Grothendieck's tame-topology programme with o-minimality could use the full 156-3 series. This page alone adds only the trivial one-dimensional model.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is an elementary sanity-check example (complements of finite subsets of a dense order). It is interesting only as evidence of the unpublished découpage axiomatics, which is documented more substantively on neighbouring pages.
transcription_corrections: 'partie modifiée' / 'position modifiée' (here and on neighbouring pages) should very likely read 'modérée' (tame); 'Modf' = 'modérées fermées'.
'On {+v+}eut[?] un tel ensemble une ligne ordonnée' likely reads 'On appelle un tel ensemble une ligne ordonnée'.
'Pb fonctions[?]' in the margin is uncertain; possibly 'Pb fonctorialité' or 'Pb fonctions'.
'divisible[?]' probably expresses density of the order.
'Modf(L) = parties finies tot. ordonnées[?]' is more likely just 'parties finies' (with the inserted 'pour les tot. ordonnés' qualifying the context).
